source.title: Scaling Behavior of Parameterized Quantum Circuits from a Lie-Algebraic Perspective

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests analogous resource-scaling behavior in parameterized quantum circuits, a setting beyond text pretraining, using regression RMSE rather than language-model pretraining cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own regression-loss scaling results for quantum circuits. It does not test language models, held-out pretraining cross-entropy, extrapolation from small language-model runs, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape effects, or downstream task predictability. Loss values are shown in figures; the text gives fitted slopes and summary results.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the scaling-law form from Kaplan et al. and applies it by analogy to parameterized quantum circuits on a toy linear-regression task. None of the versions name this kind of system. V5 extends the claim to other modalities and regimes of neural models (image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning), not variational quantum circuits. The measure is training RMSE rather than held-out loss. Each sweep spans only one to 1.5 decades. The authors state that a power-law form is not established and would need comparisons with alternative functional forms. The results show loss decreasing with resources in a different kind of system, so they are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Over the small ranges tested, the authors find that training RMSE decreases with M, P and T, with consistently negative fitted slopes. DLA and OOD saturate in the random-Pauli ansatz, while Deff tracks P closely; they propose Deff as a geometry-aware effective model size. They caution that establishing a universal power law needs broader studies and comparison with alternative functional forms.
record.recipe_differences: Uses parameterized quantum circuits and a linear regression task with RMSE, not language models trained on text and held-out cross-entropy. It studies finite resource sweeps rather than extrapolation or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

fits_no_version.finding: In random-Pauli parameterized quantum circuits on a linear-regression task (n=4 and 8 qubits), training RMSE falls with sample size M, parameter count P and SPSA iterations T. Fitted log-log slopes are small and negative, about −0.07 to −0.14, over 1–1.5 decades. DLA and OOD saturate at larger P, while the Jacobian effective dimension tracks P closely (r=0.9997).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss of parameterized quantum circuits decreases approximately as a power of data, parameter count and optimization steps, and the Jacobian effective dimension is a usable effective model-size measure.

record.problems: The experiments cover one regression task and relatively small systems (four and eight qubits), and only finite ranges of data size, model size, and optimization iterations. The authors state that broader comparisons with alternative functional forms are needed to establish a universal asymptotic power law. DLA and OOD saturate in the tested ansatz.
record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/V5 'supports' label is removed. Variational quantum circuits on a toy regression task are not the kind of system V5 names. The loss is training RMSE. Sweeps are short, and the authors explicitly decline to claim a power-law form. The decreasing loss with more training samples is measured on training loss, which is unusual and worth noting. The record's 'training compute' reading of T is loose: T is the number of optimizer iterations at fixed data.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss and its dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The loss-minimising allocation of parameters and tokens under a fixed compute budget.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests only a randomly generated Pauli-string quantum-circuit regression setting; does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or language-model pretraining.
Downstream task performance and its relationship to pretraining loss or scale.
Does not compare fitting choices or setups to establish that exponents depend on them, or report curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: parameterized unitary with randomly sampled Pauli-string generators
rows.operation_detail: Varied training sample size M and fitted log-log loss scaling.
rows.measure: Log-log RMSE scaling coefficient with respect to M
rows.locator: Section 3, Results of data scaling; Figure 1
rows.note: The paper reports decreasing loss over the tested sample-size range. Parentheses give standard deviations across independent runs.
rows.check: Subject is a 4-qubit parameterized quantum circuit on linear regression, not a language or other neural model as V1/V5 name. Loss is training RMSE, not held-out. The slope fit over M=100–100000 is not tested against non-power-law forms. Baseline 'not stated' is correct.

rows.note: The paper reports decreasing loss over the tested sample-size range. Parentheses give standard deviations across independent runs.
rows.check: Same as R1, for n=8 qubits. Training RMSE in a quantum circuit, outside every version's system.

rows.subject: parameterized unitary with randomly sampled Pauli-string generators
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter size P and fitted log-log loss scaling.
rows.measure: Log-log RMSE scaling coefficient with respect to P
rows.locator: Section 3, Results of model scaling; Figure 2
rows.note: The paper reports decreasing loss over the tested parameter-size range.
rows.check: Parameter sweep P=2–32 (1.2 decades) in a quantum circuit. The slope SD (0.084) is large relative to the mean (−0.135). Not a model kind any version names.

rows.subject: parameterized unitary with randomly sampled Pauli-string generators
rows.operation_detail: Related loss to dynamical Lie algebra dimension (DLA) across parameter sizes.
rows.measure: Log-log loss scaling coefficient with respect to DLA
rows.locator: Section 3, Results of model scaling; Figures 3 and 4
rows.note: DLA saturated at 255 for P = 16 and 32, so the authors say the fitted slope is difficult to interpret as a genuine scaling exponent.
rows.check: DLA saturates at 255 for P=16 and 32. The authors say the slope is hard to interpret as a scaling exponent, so 'partial' is wrong; the value cannot be read as an exponent.

rows.subject: parameterized unitary with randomly sampled Pauli-string generators
rows.operation_detail: Related loss to observable orbit dimension (OOD) across parameter sizes.
rows.measure: Log-log loss scaling coefficient with respect to OOD
rows.locator: Section 3, Results of model scaling; Figures 3 and 4
rows.note: OOD saturated at 128 for P = 16 and 32, so the authors say the fitted slope is difficult to interpret as a genuine scaling exponent.
rows.check: OOD saturates at 128 for P=16 and 32. As with R4, the slope is uninterpretable per the authors, so cannot_determine fits rather than partial.

rows.subject: parameterized unitary with randomly sampled Pauli-string generators
rows.operation_detail: Related loss to Jacobian effective dimension (Deff) across parameter sizes.
rows.measure: Log-log loss scaling coefficient with respect to Deff; correlation between Deff and P
rows.value: α = −0.12573 (0.08835); p-value < 0.01; Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient between Deff and P: 0.9997 (p-value < 0.01)
rows.locator: Section 3, Results of model scaling; Figures 3 and 4
rows.note: The authors report Deff remains strongly correlated with P and gives scaling behavior comparable to P.
rows.check: Combines two measures: the loss–Deff slope and the Deff–P correlation (0.9997). The correlation is a property of the proposed metric, not a loss-scaling result. Quantum-circuit system outside every version.

rows.subject: parameterized unitary with randomly sampled Pauli-string generators
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of SPSA optimization iterations T as a proxy for training compute and fitted log-log loss scaling.
rows.measure: Log-log RMSE scaling coefficient with respect to T
rows.locator: Section 3, Results of compute scaling; Figure 5
rows.note: The paper uses SPSA iteration count as a proxy for training compute and reports decreasing loss over the tested range.
rows.check: SPSA iteration count T is used as a compute proxy. This is optimization steps on a fixed M=100 dataset, i.e. training-loss convergence, not compute scaling in the V1 sense. Quantum circuit, not a version's system.
